implementation_notes: The Splitter's roles collapse into a lazy range pipeline: std::views::split yields one subrange per delimiter occurrence and std::views::chunk groups a range into fixed-size subranges, so the send loop is an ordinary for-range over a view - there is no splitter object, no part container and no materialised list. Two details bite: an ordinary string literal delimiter carries its null terminator into the pattern and never matches, so use a std::string_view literal, and split_view keeps subranges contiguous (the property that makes it usable for string splitting) where lazy_split_view does not. Prefer this form whenever the toolchain is C++20; the class-based Splitter is still justified when the split rule must be looked up at runtime from a registry of formats.
pitfalls: views::split yields subranges, not strings: constructing each part copies unless the transport can send a string_view, so keep the source buffer alive for the whole loop.
An ordinary string literal delimiter includes the terminating '\0' and never matches.
views::chunk does not pad: the last chunk is short, and consumers must tolerate it.
A view over a temporary dangles - bind the composite to a named object before adapting it.

variants.name: Coroutine generator (std::generator with co_yield)
variants.idiom_name: std::generator<Part> producing one co_yield per part
variants.implementation_notes: std::generator turns the splitter into a coroutine that produces one element per co_yield: the consumer's for-range resumes the coroutine on demand, so a huge composite is never materialised and pacing is inherited from the consumer loop. std::generator models view and input_range and composes with co_yield std::ranges::elements_of(...), which lets nested composites be flattened into one pipeline (the coroutine stack is resumed frame by frame). Choose it when on-demand production or nested flattening matters; the ranges variants stay simpler and cheaper for finite in-memory payloads.
pitfalls: The generator borrows the source buffer: the caller must keep it alive for the whole iteration, otherwise co_yield hands out views into freed memory.
std::generator is C++23; on older toolchains the same shape needs a coroutine library, not a hand-rolled promise type.
Exceptions thrown inside the coroutine surface at the consumer's increment, so error handling belongs around the for-range, not around the generator call.
